- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile (alternating ±0.33), model often underestimates or fails to anticipate sharp reversals; increase downward bias or add early warning for mean reversion.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for 3–5 days post-spike.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 60–65) after a peak, model often fails to recognize it — adjust forecast to align with recent 7–14 day moving average.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is neutral or mixed (±0.33), model often drifts toward historical mean — use sentiment-weighted smoothing: overweight recent sentiment if >0.5, underweight if <0.3.
- If true outcome is consistently below forecast for 5+ days, model may be “overconfident” — apply a downward correction of 2–5% per day until sentiment shifts or price stabilizes.
- If sentiment turns negative after a peak, model often fails to anticipate drop — add a “sentiment-trigger” rule: if sentiment drops below 0.33 within 3 days of peak, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 5 days.
